So here's my thoughts while watching this video. I heard a lot of web, html, css, python, javascript. etc... AI is pretty good at this stuff for mainly 2 reasons: 1) there is a butt load of it out there that the models have trained on and 2) it's not all that difficult to write in the first place. Harder things that come to mind are 100,000-1,000,000+ line code bases in C++ with heavy template usage. Also things like operating systems, CAD software (try writing a b-rep system with AI), game engine programming, memory management systems, EDA simulation software, medical software, etc... These are not trivial things to write. I do not think you're going to fire off 10-15 agents and have them "vibe code" any of the aforementioned projects while you take a nap or head to the beach for some R&R. In these verticals, you're going to need to know your stuff in order to bring value. That said, I don't think AI is going anywhere, it does have its limitations given how transformer based models work, but it does have its use cases. I do think we're near the peak of what we can expect from them. As technology progresses, perhaps with photonics, we'll see the costs and requirements come down a bit, but we're still a bit off from that. And maybe not as we seem to be memory bound and traffic bound at the moment, not really compute bound.

I think the conclusion drawn from the pyramid is flawed. Yes, no job was stolen when you made the pyramid, but that is only when we look at it locally. The reason you were able to make it so easily were because the cost of the required work had dropped significantly from the initial project. On a global scale, in already existing business processes and manufacturing pipelines, problems appear as regular workers no longer can compete on price per output. Instead businesses can adopt your new method of manufacturing and produce their respective items cheaper. This results in either wage drop or layoffs, as the skills required to produce such an item has become less valuable. Maybe the company could make more items by letting this augment their employees, but that only works as long as there is enough demand for the items. Other companies could be formed from this new process as some previously unworkable business models might suddenly be profitable now, but notice how you do not actually need anyone with an engineering degree to run the cad part properly (using the example here). In this case the deep technical expertise might no longer even be enough to be re-employed in a position of similar stature
